title: Depression, drugs death: Mark Dicesare's frantic final moments
article: Mark Dicesare had one thing and one thing only on his mind Nov. 6, 2015 - to end his life.
And at 1:13 p.m. that afternoon, when five police officers pumped multiple rounds into him in an open field at Kapyong Barracks on Kenaston Blvd., Dicesare fulfilled his death wish.

Dicesare, 24, was struggling in life, battling bouts of depression and substance abuse, according to a Manitoba Independent Investigation Unit report released Thursday. He was laid off from his job in Alberta, had no steady employment and was racking up unmanageable debt.
He lost his driver's licence and had a rocky relationship with his girlfriend. His close friends were concerned about his depression and other mental health issues.
And on Nov. 6, he wanted it to all go away.

That morning, still in a fog of alcohol and cocaine consumption from the night before, Dicesare demanded access to a firearm his roommate kept under his bed. The firearm was a BB gun. It wasn't even loaded. But it bore a striking resemblance to a genuine Uzi submachine gun, a prohibited weapon capable of firing multiple rounds in seconds.
Dicesare told his roommate he planned to rob a few people to get money he owed his girlfriend. In reality, he had a more destructive plan in mind.

After a brief stop at his girlfriend's home to tell her this would be the last time they would talk, Dicesare began to drive erratically at high speeds around the Tuxedo and Charleswood area, presumably trying to attract the attention of police.
He called his roommate on his cell phone to tell him he was "going out in a coffin today." His friend pleaded with him to come home. "No, it's done," Dicesare replied.

It wasn't long before Dicesare found his first police target at 12:21 p.m. while driving along Oakdale Drive in Charleswood. The female cop, a school liaison officer in a marked police vehicle, rolled down her window as Dicesare slowed his car towards hers. She thought he wanted to talk. Instead, she found herself staring down the barrel of what looked like an automatic weapon.
Dicesare fled. And the vehicle chase began.

Dicesare's girlfriend had already called 911 to alert police that her boyfriend was in distress and could be dangerous. He may have a gun, she said. Within minutes, police cruisers began flooding the area.
Apparently Dicesare wanted to leave a suicide message of sorts and made a short video of himself on his cell phone during the chase.
"Hey guys, I just want to let you guys know before I go, I um, I had a good life, OK?" he recorded. "I had fun, I uh...I'm so sorry guys..."
Dicesare pointed his gun at cops again on Grant Avenue. And with eight police cruisers now in tow, he continued to race around the neighbourhood, his gun sticking through the sunroof of his car.
The chase came to a brief stop at the corner of Willow Avenue and Doncaster Street, right outside the Rady Centre where police managed to pin Dicesare's vehicle in.
Dicesare again pointed his firearm at police. Two officers said they would have shot him right there but there were civilians and other cops in the line of fire.

The break in action didn't last long, though. Dicesare managed to squeeze out of the box police had him in and he was back on Doncaster racing towards Kapyong Barracks, where the chase ultimately came to an end.
Dicesare was pinned in again on the field beside Lipsett Hall. But this time, there was no escaping.
Police repeatedly ordered Dicesare to drop his weapon. They pleaded with him to surrender. But Dicesare had already made up his mind.
"I'm going to die today and you're going to do it," he told one officer.
"I'm sorry I have to do this to you guys," he told another. "Please shoot me in the head and make it quick."
Dicesare eventually exited his vehicle, his firearm pointing in the air and resting against his chin. This was it. His face went expressionless. He lowered the gun, aimed it directly at police.
Five officers - who had no other options - opened fire.
Dicesare was pronounced dead at 1:47 p.m.
